questions.topic: Ch 6 · National income accounting · Meaning of national income
questions.stem: National income is best described as the money value of all:

options.text: final goods and services produced by the normal residents of a country during a year
options.explanation: Correct. National income is the money value of final output of a country's normal residents over an accounting year — a flow, counting final goods only.

options.text: goods, both intermediate and final, produced in a country during a year
options.explanation: Counting intermediate goods as well as final goods would double-count. Only final goods and services are included.

options.text: wealth owned by the citizens of a country at a point in time
options.explanation: Wealth is a stock held at a point in time; national income is a flow produced over a period.

options.text: money in circulation in a country during a year
options.explanation: The stock of money is not national income. National income measures the value of output produced, not the money supply.

readLink.label: Read: National income — what it measures, §1 →

questions.sourceRef: National income = money value of final goods and services of normal residents in a year

questions.topic: Ch 6 · National income accounting · GDP definition
questions.stem: Gross Domestic Product (GDP) measures the value of output produced:

options.text: by the normal residents of a country, wherever they earn it
options.explanation: That describes GNP, the national concept. GDP is defined by territory, not residence.

options.text: within the geographical territory of a country, whoever owns the factors
options.explanation: Correct. GDP is the value of output produced inside the country's territory, regardless of who owns the factors of production.
GDP covers all producing units — private and public — not only government enterprises.
Deducting depreciation gives a NET measure (NDP). GDP is a gross figure, before depreciation.

questions.sourceRef: GDP = output within the domestic territory, before depreciation

questions.topic: Ch 6 · National income accounting · GNP and NFIA
questions.stem: Gross National Product (GNP) is obtained from GDP by:

options.text: adding net factor income from abroad
options.explanation: Correct. GNP = GDP + net factor income from abroad, the factor income residents earn abroad minus what foreigners earn at home.

options.text: subtracting net factor income from abroad
options.explanation: The adjustment is added, not subtracted. If NFIA is negative the result is smaller than GDP, but the operation is still addition.
Net indirect taxes bridge factor cost and market price, not domestic and national. The GDP-to-GNP bridge is NFIA.
Subtracting depreciation moves gross to net (GDP to NDP), not domestic to national.

questions.sourceRef: GNP = GDP + NFIA

questions.topic: Ch 6 · National income accounting · GNP from GDP
questions.stem: GDP at market price is ₹ 5,000 crore and net factor income from abroad is ₹ 200 crore. GNP at market price is:

options.explanation: Correct. GNP = GDP + NFIA = 5,000 + 200 = ₹ 5,200 crore.
This subtracts NFIA. The net factor income from abroad is added to GDP, not subtracted.
This ignores NFIA altogether. GNP differs from GDP by the net factor income from abroad.
This adds NFIA twice. GNP = 5,000 + 200 = 5,200, not 5,400.

questions.sourceRef: GNP = GDP + NFIA = 5000 + 200

questions.topic: Ch 6 · National income accounting · NNP and depreciation
questions.stem: Net National Product (NNP) at market price is obtained from GNP at market price by:

options.explanation: Depreciation is subtracted, not added, to move from a gross figure to a net one.
Correct. NNP = GNP − depreciation; the wearing-out of capital is deducted to reach the net figure.

options.text: adding net factor income from abroad
options.explanation: NFIA bridges domestic and national concepts, not gross and net. GNP is already a national figure.
Net indirect taxes bridge market price and factor cost, not gross and net. The gross-to-net step deducts depreciation.

questions.sourceRef: NNP = GNP − depreciation

questions.topic: Ch 6 · National income accounting · Depreciation
questions.stem: The difference between a gross aggregate and its matching net aggregate is:

options.explanation: NFIA is the difference between domestic and national aggregates, not gross and net.
Net indirect taxes separate market-price and factor-cost valuations, not gross and net measures.
Correct. A net aggregate equals the gross aggregate minus depreciation — the value of capital used up in production.
Transfer payments are excluded from national income altogether; they do not separate gross from net.

questions.sourceRef: Net = Gross − depreciation

questions.topic: Ch 6 · National income accounting · NNP from GNP
questions.stem: GNP at market price is ₹ 6,000 crore and depreciation is ₹ 500 crore. NNP at market price is:

options.explanation: ₹ 500 crore is the depreciation itself, not the net national product.
Correct. NNP = GNP − depreciation = 6,000 − 500 = ₹ 5,500 crore.
This adds depreciation. Moving from gross to net deducts depreciation, giving 5,500.
This deducts too much. 6,000 − 500 = 5,500, not 5,000.

questions.sourceRef: NNP = GNP − depreciation = 6000 − 500

questions.topic: Ch 6 · National income accounting · Market price vs factor cost
questions.stem: An aggregate 'at factor cost' differs from the same aggregate 'at market price' because factor cost:

options.explanation: Depreciation separates gross from net, not factor cost from market price. The valuation difference is net indirect taxes.

options.text: excludes net indirect taxes (indirect taxes minus subsidies)
options.explanation: Correct. Factor cost is what the factors actually received; it strips out net indirect taxes, so market price = factor cost + net indirect taxes.

options.text: adds net factor income from abroad
options.explanation: NFIA bridges domestic and national aggregates, not the two valuations.
The valuation basis has nothing to do with exports; it is about whether indirect taxes and subsidies are included.

readLink.label: Read: Market price and factor cost, §3 →

questions.sourceRef: Factor cost = market price − net indirect taxes

questions.topic: Ch 6 · National income accounting · Net indirect taxes
questions.stem: Indirect taxes are ₹ 700 crore and subsidies are ₹ 150 crore. Net indirect taxes are:

options.explanation: ₹ 700 crore is the indirect taxes alone. Net indirect taxes deduct the ₹ 150 crore of subsidies.
₹ 150 crore is the subsidies alone, not the net figure. Net indirect taxes = 700 − 150 = 550.
Correct. Net indirect taxes = indirect taxes − subsidies = 700 − 150 = ₹ 550 crore.
This adds subsidies to indirect taxes. Net indirect taxes subtract subsidies: 700 − 150 = 550.

readLink.label: Read: Market price and factor cost, §3 →

questions.sourceRef: Net indirect taxes = indirect taxes − subsidies = 700 − 150

questions.topic: Ch 6 · National income accounting · Market price from factor cost
questions.stem: GDP at factor cost is ₹ 4,000 crore and net indirect taxes are ₹ 600 crore. GDP at market price is:

options.explanation: This subtracts net indirect taxes. To move from factor cost up to market price you add them.
This ignores net indirect taxes. Market price exceeds factor cost by the net indirect taxes.
₹ 600 crore is the net indirect taxes, not the market-price aggregate.
Correct. Market price = factor cost + net indirect taxes = 4,000 + 600 = ₹ 4,600 crore.

readLink.label: Read: Market price and factor cost, §3 →

questions.sourceRef: Market price = factor cost + net indirect taxes = 4000 + 600

questions.topic: Ch 6 · National income accounting · National income from NNP at market price
questions.stem: NNP at market price is ₹ 4,900 crore, indirect taxes are ₹ 500 crore and subsidies are ₹ 100 crore. National Income (NNP at factor cost) is:

options.explanation: ₹ 4,900 crore is NNP at market price. National income is that figure minus net indirect taxes.
Correct. Net indirect taxes = 500 − 100 = 400; National Income = 4,900 − 400 = ₹ 4,500 crore.
This adds net indirect taxes. National income at factor cost subtracts them from NNP at market price.
This subtracts the indirect taxes only (500) and ignores subsidies. Use net indirect taxes = 500 − 100 = 400.

questions.sourceRef: NI = NNP at market price − net indirect taxes = 4900 − (500 − 100)

questions.topic: Ch 6 · National income accounting · National income defined
questions.stem: In national income accounting, the aggregate called 'National Income' is the same as:

options.explanation: GDP at market price is gross, domestic and at market price — three steps away from national income.
GNP at market price is still gross and at market price. National income is net and at factor cost.
Correct. National Income is defined as Net National Product at factor cost — the total factor income of the country's residents.
NDP at market price is a domestic, market-price figure. National income is national and at factor cost.

readLink.label: Read: National income, personal income and disposable income, §4 →

questions.sourceRef: National Income = NNP at factor cost

questions.topic: Ch 6 · National income accounting · Personal income
questions.stem: Which of the following is ADDED to national income when arriving at personal income?

options.explanation: Undistributed profits are earned but not received by households, so they are subtracted, not added.
Corporate taxes are part of income not reaching households, so they are subtracted when computing personal income.
Correct. Transfer payments (pensions, scholarships, relief) are received by households though not earned in production, so they are added to reach personal income.
Social security contributions are withheld from households, so they are subtracted, not added.

readLink.label: Read: National income, personal income and disposable income, §4 →

questions.sourceRef: Personal income = NI − undistributed profits − corporate taxes − social security + transfer payments

questions.topic: Ch 6 · National income accounting · Disposable personal income
questions.stem: Disposable personal income is equal to personal income:

options.explanation: Correct. Disposable personal income is personal income after personal (direct) taxes — what households can actually spend or save.
Direct taxes are subtracted, not added; disposable income is what remains after tax.
It is direct (personal) taxes that are deducted, not indirect taxes, which are already handled in the market-price/factor-cost step.
Transfer payments are added earlier, when moving from national income to personal income, not at the disposable-income stage.

readLink.label: Read: National income, personal income and disposable income, §4 →

questions.sourceRef: Disposable personal income = personal income − direct taxes

questions.topic: Ch 6 · National income accounting · Full aggregate chain
questions.stem: GDP at market price is ₹ 8,000 crore, net factor income from abroad is −₹ 100 crore, depreciation is ₹ 700 crore, indirect taxes are ₹ 900 crore and subsidies are ₹ 200 crore. National Income is:

options.explanation: This ignores the negative NFIA. GNP = 8,000 + (−100) = 7,900, not 8,000.
This deducts too much (for example subtracting the indirect taxes without adding back subsidies twice). The correct chain gives ₹ 6,500 crore.
₹ 7,200 crore is NNP at market price. National income deducts net indirect taxes of ₹ 700 crore as well.

questions.sourceRef: NI = GDPmp + NFIA − depreciation − net indirect taxes

questions.topic: Ch 6 · National income accounting · Nominal vs real GDP
questions.stem: Real GDP differs from nominal GDP because real GDP values output at:

options.explanation: Current-year prices give NOMINAL GDP, which rises with both output and prices. Real GDP uses base-year prices.

options.text: the prices of a fixed base year
options.explanation: Correct. Real GDP values output at constant base-year prices, so it rises only when output actually rises — inflation is stripped out.

options.text: factor cost rather than market price
options.explanation: The real–nominal distinction is about the year of the prices used, not about factor cost versus market price.
Real GDP uses the country's own base-year prices, not world prices.

readLink.label: Read: Nominal GDP, real GDP and the deflator, §6 →

questions.sourceRef: Real GDP values output at constant base-year prices

questions.topic: Ch 6 · National income accounting · GDP deflator
questions.stem: Nominal GDP is ₹ 6,000 crore and real GDP is ₹ 5,000 crore. The GDP deflator is:

options.explanation: This inverts the ratio (real ÷ nominal). The deflator is nominal over real, times 100.
A deflator of 100 would mean nominal equals real. Here nominal exceeds real, so the deflator is above 100.
130 is not the ratio of the two figures. (6,000 ÷ 5,000) × 100 = 120.
Correct. GDP deflator = (nominal ÷ real) × 100 = (6,000 ÷ 5,000) × 100 = 120.

readLink.label: Read: Nominal GDP, real GDP and the deflator, §6 →

questions.sourceRef: GDP deflator = (nominal ÷ real) × 100 = 6000/5000 × 100

questions.topic: Ch 6 · National income accounting · Real GDP from deflator
questions.stem: Nominal GDP is ₹ 7,200 crore and the GDP deflator is 120. Real GDP is:

options.explanation: Correct. Real GDP = (nominal ÷ deflator) × 100 = (7,200 ÷ 120) × 100 = ₹ 6,000 crore.
This multiplies nominal by the deflator/100 instead of dividing. Real GDP = 7,200 ÷ 1.2 = 6,000.
₹ 7,200 crore is the nominal figure. With a deflator above 100, real GDP is smaller than nominal.
6,600 is not 7,200 ÷ 1.2. Dividing nominal by the deflator (as a fraction of 100) gives 6,000.

readLink.label: Read: Nominal GDP, real GDP and the deflator, §6 →

questions.sourceRef: Real GDP = (nominal ÷ deflator) × 100 = 7200/120 × 100

questions.topic: Ch 6 · National income accounting · Deflator interpretation
questions.stem: In the base year itself, the GDP deflator is always:

options.explanation: A deflator of 0 has no meaning. In the base year nominal and real GDP are equal, giving a deflator of 100.
Correct. In the base year, output is valued at base-year prices for both measures, so nominal = real and the deflator = (nominal ÷ real) × 100 = 100.
A deflator above 100 signals prices above base-year levels, which cannot happen in the base year itself.
A deflator below 100 signals prices below base-year levels; in the base year the deflator is exactly 100.

readLink.label: Read: Nominal GDP, real GDP and the deflator, §6 →

questions.sourceRef: Base year: nominal = real, deflator = 100

questions.topic: Ch 6 · National income accounting · Per capita income
questions.stem: National Income is ₹ 5,00,000 crore and the population is 25 crore. Per capita income is:

options.explanation: 25,000 uses the wrong divisor. Dividing 5,00,000 crore by 25 crore gives 20,000.
₹ 5,00,000 crore is the total national income, not the income per head.
Correct. Per capita income = National Income ÷ population = 5,00,000 ÷ 25 = ₹ 20,000 per person.
12,500 does not follow from 5,00,000 ÷ 25. The correct quotient is 20,000.

questions.sourceRef: Per capita income = National Income ÷ population = 500000/25

questions.topic: Ch 6 · National income accounting · Circular flow
questions.stem: In the circular flow of income, a four-sector economy adds which sector to the three-sector model?

options.explanation: Households are present from the two-sector model onward; they are not the sector added at the four-sector stage.
The government is added at the three-sector stage. The four-sector model adds one more sector beyond that.

options.text: The foreign sector (rest of the world)
options.explanation: Correct. The four-sector model adds the foreign sector, which injects income through exports and withdraws it through imports.
Firms are present from the two-sector model. The four-sector model adds the rest of the world.

readLink.label: Read: The circular flow of income, §8 →

questions.sourceRef: Four-sector = two-sector + government + foreign sector

questions.topic: Ch 6 · National income accounting · Leakages and injections
questions.stem: Which of the following is a 'leakage' from the circular flow of income?

options.explanation: Investment is an injection — it puts income into the flow, not takes it out.
Government spending is an injection into the circular flow, not a leakage.
Exports are an injection — foreign spending on domestic output adds to the flow.
Correct. Saving is a leakage: it is income withdrawn from the flow rather than spent on output. Taxes and imports are the other leakages.

readLink.label: Read: The circular flow of income, §8 →

questions.sourceRef: Leakages: saving, taxes, imports; injections: investment, government spending, exports

questions.topic: Ch 6 · Methods of measurement · Value added and double counting
questions.stem: The value added method avoids 'double counting' by:

options.text: adding the full value of output at every stage of production
options.explanation: Adding full output at every stage is exactly the double-counting error, because intermediate goods get counted again and again.

options.text: counting only the value added by each producing unit (output minus intermediate consumption)
options.explanation: Correct. Value added = output − intermediate consumption; summing value added counts each good's value only once.

options.text: counting only the output of the final firm
options.explanation: The method sums value added across all firms, not the output of the final firm alone, though both happen to equal the final value.
Transfer payments are not production and are excluded from all methods; they have nothing to do with avoiding double counting.

questions.sourceRef: Value added = output − intermediate consumption; avoids double counting

questions.topic: Ch 6 · Methods of measurement · Expenditure method
questions.stem: By the expenditure method, with C = ₹ 3,000 crore, I = ₹ 800 crore, G = ₹ 1,200 crore, exports X = ₹ 500 crore and imports M = ₹ 400 crore, GDP at market price is:

options.explanation: This adds imports instead of subtracting them. Net exports = X − M = 500 − 400 = 100, giving 5,100.
This omits net exports altogether. Add X − M = 100 to reach 5,100.
This subtracts exports as well as imports. Only imports are subtracted; net exports add 100 here.

questions.topic: Ch 6 · Methods of measurement · Income method
questions.stem: By the income method, with compensation of employees ₹ 2,500 crore, rent ₹ 400 crore, interest ₹ 300 crore, profit ₹ 600 crore and mixed income ₹ 700 crore, domestic income (NDP at factor cost) is:

options.explanation: 5,000 overstates the total. The five factor incomes sum to 4,500, not 5,000.
Correct. Domestic income = 2,500 + 400 + 300 + 600 + 700 = ₹ 4,500 crore.
This omits one component (the mixed income of ₹ 700 crore). All five factor incomes are summed.
This omits one component (the profit of ₹ 600 crore). The full sum is 4,500.

questions.sourceRef: Domestic income = rent + wages + interest + profit + mixed income = 2500+400+300+600+700

questions.topic: Ch 6 · Methods of measurement · Income method components
questions.stem: Under the income method, the income of a self-employed shopkeeper, in which wages, rent, interest and profit cannot be separated, is recorded as:

options.explanation: Net indirect taxes are a valuation adjustment, not a factor income. The shopkeeper's earnings are mixed income.
Compensation of employees is the wage of hired labour; the self-employed shopkeeper is not an employee.
Correct. The income of the self-employed, where the factor rewards cannot be separated, is recorded as mixed income.
A transfer payment is received without production; the shopkeeper earns income by producing and selling, so it is a factor income.

questions.sourceRef: Mixed income = income of the self-employed

questions.topic: Ch 6 · Methods of measurement · Expenditure components
questions.stem: In the expenditure method formula GDP = C + I + G + (X − M), the term 'I' stands for:

options.text: spending on new capital goods and additions to stock (gross domestic investment)
options.explanation: Correct. I is gross domestic investment — spending by firms on new capital goods and additions to inventory.

options.text: the purchase of shares and bonds by households
options.explanation: Buying financial assets is not investment in national income; I means spending on new physical capital goods.
Interest is a factor income in the income method, not the investment term in the expenditure method.
Imports are captured in the (X − M) term. I is domestic investment spending.

questions.sourceRef: I = gross domestic investment (new capital goods + stock)

questions.topic: Ch 6 · Methods of measurement · Precautions (double counting)
questions.stem: To avoid double counting in the value added or expenditure method, one must exclude the value of:

options.explanation: Government final consumption is a genuine component of expenditure, not a double-counting item.
Exports are part of final expenditure; they are not excluded to avoid double counting.
Final goods are precisely what national income counts. It is intermediate goods that must be excluded.
Correct. Intermediate goods (inputs bought from other firms) are excluded, because their value is already embodied in the final good.

readLink.label: Read: Precautions and reconciling the methods, §12 →

questions.sourceRef: Exclude intermediate goods to avoid double counting

questions.topic: Ch 6 · Methods of measurement · Precautions (transfer payments)
questions.stem: Which of the following is a transfer payment that must be EXCLUDED from national income?

options.explanation: Rent is a factor income for the use of land and is included in national income.
Profit is a factor income (the reward of enterprise) and is included in national income.

options.text: Wages paid to a factory worker
options.explanation: Wages are a factor income earned in production and are included in national income.

options.text: An old-age pension paid by the government
options.explanation: Correct. A pension is a transfer payment — income received without any current production in return — so it is excluded from national income.

readLink.label: Read: Precautions and reconciling the methods, §12 →

questions.sourceRef: Transfer payments (pensions) excluded from national income

questions.topic: Ch 6 · Methods of measurement · Financial transactions
questions.stem: The purchase of existing shares on the stock exchange is excluded from national income because it is:

options.text: a financial transaction, not production of a good or service
options.explanation: Correct. Buying existing shares transfers ownership of an existing asset; nothing is produced, so it is excluded from national income.

options.text: a form of gross domestic investment
options.explanation: Investment in national income means new capital goods, not the buying of shares, which is a financial transfer.
A share purchase by a household is not government spending; it is a financial transaction that is excluded.

options.text: a factor income like rent or wages
options.explanation: A share purchase is not a factor income. Dividends might be, but buying the share itself is a financial transfer.

readLink.label: Read: Precautions and reconciling the methods, §12 →

questions.sourceRef: Financial transactions (buying shares) excluded — not production

questions.topic: Ch 6 · National income and welfare · Limitations
questions.stem: Which of the following is a limitation of national income as a measure of economic welfare?

options.text: It measures leisure and environmental quality precisely
options.explanation: National income does NOT measure leisure or environmental costs; omitting them is one of its limitations.

options.text: It counts pollution as a cost against output
options.explanation: National income does not net off pollution and resource depletion; failing to do so is a limitation, not a strength.

options.text: It captures the exact distribution of income among households
options.explanation: This is the opposite of the truth: per capita income is an average that hides the distribution of income, which is a limitation.

options.text: It ignores the distribution of income and non-market production
options.explanation: Correct. National income hides inequality, leaves out non-market production (such as a homemaker's work) and ignores externalities, so it is an imperfect welfare measure.

readLink.label: Read: National income as a measure of welfare, §13 →

questions.sourceRef: Limitations: distribution hidden, non-market output ignored, externalities uncounted

questions.topic: Ch 6 · Methods of measurement · Factor income vs transfer
questions.stem: Which of the following is a factor income that IS included in national income?

options.text: A gift received from a relative
options.explanation: A gift is a transfer, not payment for a factor service, so it is excluded from national income.
Unemployment relief is a transfer payment, excluded from national income because no output is produced in return.

options.text: A scholarship paid to a student
options.explanation: A scholarship is a transfer payment, received without production, and is excluded from national income.

options.text: Interest received on a loan to a business
options.explanation: Correct. Interest is the factor reward of capital, earned in production, so it is a factor income included in national income.

questions.sourceRef: Factor incomes (interest) included; transfers excluded

questions.topic: Ch 6 · National income accounting · NFIA meaning
questions.stem: Net factor income from abroad (NFIA) is:

options.explanation: Indirect taxes minus subsidies is net indirect taxes, a valuation adjustment, not NFIA.

options.text: total foreign aid received in a year
options.explanation: Foreign aid is a transfer, not a factor income. NFIA concerns factor incomes across borders.
Exports minus imports is net exports of goods and services, part of the expenditure method — not NFIA, which is about factor income.

options.text: factor income earned by residents abroad minus factor income earned by foreigners at home
options.explanation: Correct. NFIA is the factor income (wages, interest, rent, profit) residents earn abroad minus that earned by foreigners within the country.

questions.sourceRef: NFIA = factor income of residents abroad − factor income of foreigners at home

questions.topic: Ch 6 · National income accounting · Disposable income identity
questions.stem: Disposable personal income is used by households in exactly two ways. These are:

options.explanation: Correct. A household either spends its disposable income (consumption) or does not (saving), so disposable income = consumption + saving.
Taxes are already deducted to arrive at disposable income; what remains is split between consumption and saving.
Households consume and save; investment is a decision of firms, not the use of household disposable income.
Transfer payments are receipts, not a use of income. Disposable income is used for consumption and saving.

readLink.label: Read: National income, personal income and disposable income, §4 →

questions.sourceRef: Disposable income = consumption + saving

questions.topic: Ch 6 · Keynesian theory · Aggregate demand
questions.stem: In the simple two-sector Keynesian model, aggregate demand consists of:

options.explanation: Correct. In the two-sector model aggregate demand is planned consumption plus planned investment, C + I.
Aggregate demand also includes investment. Consumption alone is not the whole of planned spending.
Saving is a leakage, not a component of aggregate demand. Aggregate demand is C + I.

options.text: government spending and net exports only
options.explanation: Those appear in the fuller model; in the two-sector model aggregate demand is C + I.

readLink.label: Read: Aggregate demand and aggregate supply, §14 →

questions.sourceRef: Two-sector aggregate demand = C + I

questions.topic: Ch 6 · Keynesian theory · Consumption function
questions.stem: In the consumption function C = a + bY, the term 'a' represents:

options.text: autonomous consumption — the consumption at zero income
options.explanation: Correct. 'a' is autonomous consumption, the amount consumed even when income is zero, financed by past savings or borrowing.
The marginal propensity to consume is 'b', the slope of the line, not the intercept 'a'.
'a' is autonomous consumption, not saving. At zero income the household dis-saves by the amount 'a'.
Investment is a separate variable; 'a' is the intercept of the consumption function, autonomous consumption.

questions.sourceRef: C = a + bY; a = autonomous consumption

questions.topic: Ch 6 · Keynesian theory · APC
questions.stem: At an income of ₹ 1,000 crore, consumption is ₹ 800 crore. The average propensity to consume (APC) is:

options.explanation: Correct. APC = C ÷ Y = 800 ÷ 1,000 = 0.8.
1.25 inverts the ratio (Y ÷ C). APC is consumption divided by income, 800 ÷ 1,000 = 0.8.
0.2 is the average propensity to SAVE (200 ÷ 1,000), not the APC. APC = 800 ÷ 1,000 = 0.8.
0.08 misplaces the decimal. 800 ÷ 1,000 = 0.8, not 0.08.

questions.topic: Ch 6 · Keynesian theory · MPC
questions.stem: When income rises by ₹ 100 crore, consumption rises by ₹ 60 crore. The marginal propensity to consume (MPC) is:

options.explanation: 0.4 is the marginal propensity to SAVE (40 ÷ 100). MPC = 60 ÷ 100 = 0.6.
0.06 misplaces the decimal. 60 ÷ 100 = 0.6, not 0.06.
Correct. MPC = ΔC ÷ ΔY = 60 ÷ 100 = 0.6.
1.67 inverts the ratio (ΔY ÷ ΔC). MPC is the change in consumption over the change in income, 60 ÷ 100 = 0.6.

questions.sourceRef: MPC = ΔC ÷ ΔY = 60/100

questions.topic: Ch 6 · Keynesian theory · Range of MPC
questions.stem: The marginal propensity to consume (MPC) normally lies:

options.explanation: Correct. An extra rupee of income raises consumption, but by less than a rupee (part is saved), so 0 < MPC < 1.
An MPC above 1 would mean consumption rises by more than the extra income, which is not the normal case.
A negative MPC would mean consumption falls when income rises, contrary to the consumption function.
MPC = 1 would mean all extra income is consumed and none saved; normally MPC is a fraction between 0 and 1.

questions.sourceRef: 0 < MPC < 1

questions.topic: Ch 6 · Keynesian theory · APS
questions.stem: At an income of ₹ 2,000 crore, consumption is ₹ 1,500 crore. The average propensity to save (APS) is:

options.explanation: 0.75 is the average propensity to CONSUME (1,500 ÷ 2,000). APS = 1 − APC = 0.25.
0.5 does not match the figures. Saving of 500 on income of 2,000 gives APS = 0.25.
0.2 is not 500 ÷ 2,000. The average propensity to save here is 0.25.
Correct. Saving = 2,000 − 1,500 = 500; APS = S ÷ Y = 500 ÷ 2,000 = 0.25 (and indeed APC = 0.75, so APC + APS = 1).

questions.topic: Ch 6 · Keynesian theory · MPS from MPC
questions.stem: If the marginal propensity to consume is 0.75, the marginal propensity to save (MPS) is:

options.explanation: 0.5 does not satisfy MPC + MPS = 1. With MPC = 0.75, MPS = 0.25.
Correct. MPS = 1 − MPC = 1 − 0.75 = 0.25, because MPC + MPS = 1.
0.75 is the MPC itself. The MPS is 1 − MPC = 0.25.
1.33 inverts the MPC. MPS is 1 − MPC = 0.25, not 1 ÷ MPC.

questions.topic: Ch 6 · Keynesian theory · MPC + MPS identity
questions.stem: The sum of the marginal propensity to consume and the marginal propensity to save (MPC + MPS) always equals:

options.explanation: MPC + MPS is a pure ratio equal to 1; it is unrelated to the level of income.
The propensities are positive fractions that add to 1, not to 0.
Correct. Any extra income is either consumed or saved, so MPC + MPS = 1 (and likewise APC + APS = 1).
The multiplier is 1 ÷ MPS, a separate quantity. MPC + MPS is always 1.

questions.sourceRef: MPC + MPS = 1

questions.topic: Ch 6 · Keynesian theory · Multiplier from MPC
questions.stem: If the marginal propensity to consume is 0.8, the investment multiplier is:

options.explanation: 1.25 is 1 ÷ MPC (1 ÷ 0.8). The multiplier is 1 ÷ (1 − MPC) = 1 ÷ 0.2 = 5.
4 would follow from MPC = 0.75. With MPC = 0.8, k = 1 ÷ 0.2 = 5.
0.8 is the MPC itself, not the multiplier. k = 1 ÷ (1 − 0.8) = 5.

questions.topic: Ch 6 · Keynesian theory · Multiplier from MPS
questions.stem: If the marginal propensity to save is 0.25, the investment multiplier is:

options.explanation: 5 would follow from MPS = 0.2. With MPS = 0.25, k = 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4.
1.33 is 1 ÷ 0.75, using MPC by mistake. The multiplier is 1 ÷ MPS = 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4.
Correct. k = 1 ÷ MPS = 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4.
0.25 is the MPS itself. The multiplier is its reciprocal, 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4.

questions.topic: Ch 6 · Keynesian theory · Change in income from multiplier
questions.stem: The marginal propensity to consume is 0.75 and investment rises by ₹ 200 crore. The resulting increase in income is:

options.explanation: 250 does not follow from the multiplier. With k = 4, ΔY = 4 × 200 = 800.
₹ 200 crore is the rise in investment itself. Income rises by a multiple of it: ΔY = 4 × 200 = 800.
1,000 would use a multiplier of 5 (MPC = 0.8). Here MPC = 0.75, so k = 4 and ΔY = 800.

questions.topic: Ch 6 · Keynesian theory · Equilibrium income
questions.stem: In a two-sector economy the consumption function is C = 100 + 0.8Y and autonomous investment is ₹ 100 crore. The equilibrium level of income is:

options.explanation: ₹ 200 crore is total autonomous spending (a + I). Equilibrium income is that divided by (1 − MPC): 200 ÷ 0.2 = 1,000.
800 does not solve Y = 100 + 0.8Y + 100. Solving gives 0.2Y = 200, so Y = 1,000.
250 does not satisfy the equilibrium equation. The correct income is ₹ 1,000 crore.

questions.topic: Ch 6 · Keynesian theory · Equilibrium condition S = I
questions.stem: In the simple Keynesian two-sector model, the equilibrium level of income can equivalently be found where:

options.explanation: Correct. Since Y = C + S and equilibrium is Y = C + I, it follows that S = I — the leakage equals the injection.
There is no equilibrium requirement that saving equal consumption. Equilibrium requires saving to equal investment.
Equilibrium does not require C = I. The condition is S = I (or equivalently Y = C + I).
Y = C would mean zero saving and zero investment. In general equilibrium is Y = C + I, i.e. S = I.

questions.sourceRef: Equilibrium: Y = C + I ⇔ S = I

questions.topic: Ch 6 · Keynesian theory · Paradox of thrift
questions.stem: The paradox of thrift states that when all households try to save more at the same time:

options.explanation: The paradox is about output and saving in a world of idle resources, not a general price rise.

options.text: investment automatically rises to match the extra saving
options.explanation: There is no automatic rise in investment; the attempt to save more reduces demand and income instead.

options.text: total saving rises sharply and income rises with it
options.explanation: This is the opposite of the paradox. When everyone tries to save more, spending falls and income falls, so total saving need not rise.

options.text: aggregate demand falls, income falls through the multiplier, and total saving may not rise
options.explanation: Correct. A general attempt to save more cuts consumption and aggregate demand; income falls by a multiple, so total saving does not increase and may even fall.

questions.sourceRef: Paradox of thrift: general attempt to save more lowers income, total saving need not rise

questions.topic: Ch 6 · Keynesian theory · Consumption from the function
questions.stem: The consumption function is C = 200 + 0.6Y. At an income of ₹ 2,000 crore, planned consumption is:

options.explanation: 1,300 does not match the function. C = 200 + 1,200 = 1,400.
₹ 2,000 crore is the income, not consumption. C = 200 + 0.6 × 2,000 = 1,400.
₹ 1,200 crore is only the induced part (0.6 × 2,000). Autonomous consumption of ₹ 200 crore must be added, giving 1,400.

questions.topic: Ch 6 · Keynesian theory · Multiplier and MPC relationship
questions.stem: Other things equal, the investment multiplier is larger when the marginal propensity to consume is:

options.explanation: The MPC is a fraction between 0 and 1; it is not negative, and a larger MPC (not a negative one) raises the multiplier.
Correct. A larger MPC means a smaller MPS, so k = 1 ÷ MPS is larger — more of each round of income is passed on as further spending.
A smaller MPC means a larger MPS and a smaller multiplier, the opposite of what is asked.
With MPC = 0 all extra income is saved and the multiplier is just 1 — the smallest, not the largest.

questions.sourceRef: Larger MPC → smaller MPS → larger multiplier k = 1/MPS
